{{short description|Japanese mathematician}}
{{family name hatnote|Sakabe|lang=Japanese}}

{{nihongo|'''Sakabe Kōhan'''|坂部 廣胖||1759 – September 16, 1824}}<!-- also known as Chugaku? --> was a Japanese [[mathematician]] in the [[Edo period]].<ref>Smith, David. (1914). {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|''A History of Japanese Mathematics,'' pp. 208–213. |page=208}}</ref>

Sakabe served for a time in the Fire Department of the shogunate, but he resigned that position to become a ''[[rōnin]]'' or masterless samurai.  He spent the rest of this life in study, in teaching, and in promoting mathematics education in Japan.<ref name="smith208">Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|p. 208. |page=208}}</ref>

Sakabe was a student of [[Ajima Naonobu]].<ref>Hatashi, T. [Hayashi Tsuruichi?] "The Conic Sections in the Old Japanese Mathematics," {{Google books|v8A0AAAAIAAJ|''The American Mathematical Monthly,'' Vol. 13, No. 10 (October 1906), pp. 173–174.|page=173}}</ref><ref name="hayashi120">Hayashi, Tsuruichi. (1907). "A Brief history of the Japanese Mathematics,"  {{Google books|k7LxAAAAMAAJ|''Nieuw archief voor wiskunde'' ("New Archive of Mathematics"), pp. 120.|page=120}}</ref>

Sakabe investigated some European and Chinese works which had appeared in Japan, but his general method was later construed to be innovative, clarified and thus improved.<ref>Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|p. 213. |page=213}}</ref> Foreign influence shows itself indirectly some of his published work.<ref name="smith266">Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|p. 266. |page=266}}</ref>

Sakabe's ''Sampo Tenzan Shinan-roku'' (''Treatise on Tenzan Algebra'') in 1810 was the first published work in Japan proposing the use of [[Common logarithm|logarithmic tables]]. He explained that "these tables save much labor, [but] they are but little known for the reason that they have never been printed in our country."<ref name="smith268">Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|pp. 268–270. |page=268}}</ref>  Sakabe's proposal would not be realized until twenty years after his death when the first extensive logarithmic table was published in 1844 by [[Koide Shuke]].<ref name="smith270">Smith, {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|pp. 268–270. |page=270}}</ref>

In Sakabe's ''Treatise on Tenzan Algebra'', mathematical problems are arranged in order from easy problems to difficult ones. The text presents a method for finding the length of a circumference and the length an arc of an [[ellipse]]. This was the first appearance of the problems pertaining to ellipses in printed books in Japan.<ref>Hayashi, {{Google books|k7LxAAAAMAAJ|p. 121.|page=121}}</ref>

==Selected works==
In a statistical overview derived from writings by and about Harry Smith Parkes, [[OCLC]]/[[WorldCat]] encompasses roughly 10+ works in 10+ publications in 1 language and 10+ library holdings.<ref>[http://www.oclc.org/research/activities/identities/default.htm  WorldCat Identities]: [http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-nr2003-21079  坂部広胖 1759-1824]</ref>
{{dynamic list}}
* 1795 — ''Shinsen Tetsujutsu''<ref name="smith208"/>
* 1802 — ''Kaiujutsu-keima'' (''Considerations on the theory of the polygon'')<ref name="smith208"/>
* 1803 — ''Rippō-eijiku'', method for finding cube root<ref name="hayashi120"/>
* 1810 — {{nihongo|'' Tenzan Shinan-roku''|點竄指南錄}} [http://www.worldcat.org/search?q=no:%22057236896%22  OCLC 22057236896], ''Treatise on Tenzan Algebra''<ref name="smith268"/>
* 1812 — ''Kwanki-kodo-shōhō'', measurement of spherical arcs and trigonometrical tables<ref>Hayashi, {{Google books|k7LxAAAAMAAJ|p. 122.|page=122}}</ref>
* 1816 — {{nihongo|''Kairo Anshin-roku''|海路安心錄}} [http://www.worldcat.org/search?q=no:%22122810576%22  OCLC 122810576], theory of navigation applying the spherical astronomy of the West<ref name="smith266"/>
